summary: This document defines STAMP extensions for Segment Routing networks, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6. It builds on the optional extensions in RFC 8972 to extend the Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol described in RFC 8762.

eli5.summary: You throw a ball and time how long it takes to come back. This adds ways to do that across the special routes Segment Routing networks use.

subtitle: Two STAMP extensions let Segment Routing networks name the intended reflector and choose the return path of a measurement reply.

tldr.problem: In Segment Routing networks, a STAMP Session-Sender may need to address a node by a non-routable address, and may need the reply to travel a specific return path, such as the same path or link.
tldr.mechanism: Two new STAMP TLVs: the Destination Node Address TLV (type 9) names the intended Session-Reflector, and the Return Path TLV (type 10) carries sub-TLVs for a control code, a return address, or an SR-MPLS or SRv6 segment list.
tldr.outcome: Operators can measure delay and loss along SR paths with controlled return paths, within a single administrative domain. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9503 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends RFC 8762 and RFC 8972 for SR-MPLS and SRv6 networks.

sections.title: STAMP in Segment Routing Networks
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) uses source routing, and works over MPLS (SR-MPLS) and IPv6 (SRv6). SR Policies steer traffic through user-defined paths using a stack of segments. Measuring performance, to back Service Level Agreements, is an essential requirement.

The Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP, RFC 8762) measures metrics in IP networks without a control channel to pre-signal session parameters. RFC 8972 defines optional TLV extensions. This RFC uses those TLVs so that test packets can use the same set of links and nodes in both directions.
sections.eli5: STAMP is a way to time how long a message takes to go there and back. This document adds tricks for special roads in big networks.

sections.title: Sender, Reflector and Four Timestamps
sections.content:
In the reference topology the Session-Sender S1 sends a test packet and the Session-Reflector R1 sends back a reply. S1 adds timestamp T1 on transmit and T4 on receive. R1 adds T2 on receive and T3 on transmit.

S1 and R1 may be connected by a link (a physical interface, virtual link, Link Aggregation Group, or LAG member) or by an SR path, such as an SR Policy on S1 (the head-end) toward R1 (the tail-end). The reply may return on the same path or on a different one.
sections.eli5: You stamp the time when you throw, your friend stamps when they catch and when they throw back, and you stamp when it returns.

sections.title: The Destination Node Address TLV
sections.content:
A Session-Sender may need to send test packets to a destination address that is not a routable address of the Session-Reflector, for example when the packet is tunneled. The Destination Node Address TLV (type 9) carries the address of the intended reflector, as IPv4 (length 4) or IPv6 (length 16).

If the carried address is one of the reflector's addresses, it SHOULD be used as the Source Address of the reply. If this TLV is sent, the SSID MUST also be sent. A reflector that recognizes the TLV MUST set the U flag to 1 in the reply if it determines it is not the intended destination, and in that case it does not use that address as the reply's source. Otherwise it MUST set the U flag to 0.
sections.eli5: The packet carries a note saying who it is meant for. If the wrong person catches it, they mark it as not for them.

sections.title: The Return Path TLV
sections.content:
For end-to-end SR paths, the reflector may need to reply on a specific Return Path. Putting it in the test packet (type 10) avoids signaling and keeping dynamic SR state for each STAMP session on the reflector. This matters for a stateless reflector, which otherwise has no hint how to return a packet on a specific path, for example in an ECMP environment. A stateful reflector, by contrast, needs configuration that matches all sender parameters.

A Session-Sender MUST NOT insert more than one Return Path TLV. A reflector that supports it MUST process only the first and ignore the rest, and MUST reply using the return path received if no error occurred. It MUST set the U flag to 1 in the reply if it cannot use the return path, and to 0 otherwise.
sections.eli5: You can write on the ball which road your friend must use to send it back, so your friend does not have to remember anything.

sections.title: Return Path Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Return Path TLV holds sub-TLVs. A TLV MUST NOT contain more than one control code, return address or segment list sub-TLV, and MUST NOT mix a control code with a return address or segment list. It MAY contain both a return address and a segment list.

  • Control Code (type 1, length 4): Control Code Flags with a Reply Request flag at bit 31. Value 0x0 means no reply: the reflector terminates the packet, giving one-way measurement. Value 0x1 means reply on the same incoming link in the reverse direction. Other bits are reserved, sent as 0 and ignored. Other sub-TLVs MUST be ignored.
  • Return Address (type 2, length 4 for IPv4 or 16 for IPv6): send the reply to this address instead of the sender's source address.
  • SR-MPLS Label Stack (type 3): 32-bit label stack entries with a 20-bit label, 3-bit TC, 1-bit S and 8-bit TTL. Length modulo 4 MUST be 0.
  • SRv6 Segment List (type 4): 128-bit IPv6 addresses. Length modulo 16 MUST be 0.

A sender MUST insert only one segment list sub-TLV, with at least one segment, in network order, and the reflector processes only the first. A segment list could carry just a Binding SID of the return policy, which is local to the reflector; how it is signaled to the sender is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The return instructions can be: do not send it back, send it back the way it came, send it to another address, or follow this exact list of turns.

sections.title: Interoperability with TWAMP Light
sections.content:
This document adds nothing beyond the TWAMP Light interoperability considerations in Section 4.6 of RFC 8762. Two combinations are possible: a STAMP Session-Sender with a TWAMP Light Session-Reflector, and the reverse.

If a STAMP Session-Sender uses any extension from this document, a TWAMP Light Session-Reflector sees it as the Packet Padding field.
sections.eli5: An older player who does not know the new tricks just treats the extra notes as filler and plays on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8762 and RFC 8972 also apply, including authenticated mode and HMAC integrity protection. STAMP uses a well-known UDP port, which could be a target for denial of service or aid on-path attacks, so Section 6 of RFC 8545 applies too. A sender can validate timestamps in replies, for example that T2 is later than T1.

The extensions are intended for a single network administrative domain, where the operator provisions the sender, reflector and return path. They could aid address spoofing, such as a Return Path IP Address different from the sender's address. The reflector MAY drop the packet if it cannot tell whether that address is local to the sender, and the operator may provision it, for example in an access control list.
sections.eli5: Use these tricks only inside your own network, where you control who plays, and be careful that nobody tricks the catcher into sending the ball to a stranger.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated TLV types 9 (Destination Node IPv4 or IPv6 Address) and 10 (Return Path) in the STAMP TLV Types registry from RFC 8972. It also created the Return Path Sub-TLV Types registry: 1 through 175 by IETF Review, 176 through 239 First Come First Served, 240 through 251 Experimental Use, and 252 through 254 Private Use. Values 0 and 255 are reserved.

A Return Path Control Code Flags registry was created too, with Reply Request allocated at bit 31.
sections.eli5: Official lists were made so every new kind of note gets its own number.
